blocks.content: Introduction
Imagine your OrderService already works with three required dependencies. Now you add a new FraudDetectionService, but only a few enterprise customers actually use it.
If you put it in the constructor, every place that creates OrderService suddenly breaks and must provide this new dependency, even though most customers don't need it.
This raises an important question:
Is this dependency required for the object to work, or is it genuinely optional?
The answer determines whether you should use constructor injection or setter injection.

Note

Real-Life Analogy

Think of buying a car.

An engine is required. A car without an engine isn't a valid car, so it must be installed before the car leaves the factory. This is like constructor injection.

A roof rack is optional. The car works perfectly without it, and you can add it later if needed. This is like setter injection.

Required dependencies belong in the constructor. Optional dependencies can be added later through setters.

blocks.content: 1. Understanding the Two Styles

Constructor Injection provides dependencies when the object is created. The object cannot exist without these dependencies, making them part of the object's required contract. Since they never change, they can also be made immutable.

Setter Injection provides dependencies after the object has already been created. The object can exist without these dependencies for some time, making them optional, configurable, or replaceable while the application is running.
<u>What each one actually costs and buys you</u>
blocks.text: <u>What each one actually costs and buys you</u>

blocks.content: 1. Constructor Injection
The object is fully valid the moment it is created because all required dependencies are provided upfront. There is no time where the object can exist in a half-configured state.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1782675354641-246276824.png

The dependency can be stored in a final or immutable field because it never changes during the object's lifetime. If a required dependency is missing, the error happens immediately during object creation rather than later at runtime.

The downside is that the constructor grows as more required dependencies are added. A constructor with too many parameters is often a sign that the class has too many responsibilities and should probably be split into smaller classes.
2. Setter Injection
The object can be created before all dependencies are provided. This makes the dependency genuinely optional, allows it to be configured later, or even replaced while the object is already in use.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1782675354870-944756018.png

Because the dependency is set after construction, there is a real period where the object exists but the dependency has not been provided yet. A caller can forget to call the setter, and the bug only appears later when that code path executes.

Since the dependency may be changed after the object is created, it usually cannot be stored in a final or immutable field. This approach gives more flexibility but provides weaker guarantees that the object is fully configured.
2. Real-life example: Fixing the OrderService from the story
blocks.text: 2. Real-life example: Fixing the OrderService from the story

blocks.content: The fix isn't to abandon constructor injection the repository and pricing engine genuinely are required, and should stay exactly where they were in the previous lesson.
The fix is recognizing that fraud detection is a different kind of dependency entirely, and giving it the injection style that matches what it actually is.
Two dependencies, Two different contracts
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1782675355113-713200029.png
This diagram shows that not all dependencies are the same. Some are required for the object to work, while others are optional.

OrderRepository and PricingEngine are required dependencies. OrderService cannot function without them, so they are provided through the constructor. The object becomes fully valid as soon as it is created.

FraudDetectionService is an optional dependency. Most customers may never use it, so forcing everyone to provide it in the constructor would add unnecessary complexity. Instead, it is provided through a setter only when needed.
The main idea is simple:
["Required dependencies → Constructor Injection","Optional dependencies → Setter Injection"]
The solid line in the diagram represents a required dependency that must exist at creation time, while the dashed line represents an optional dependency that can be added later.
Fix in code

Every existing call site that constructs anOrderServicecompiles and runs completely unchanged the fix didn't break a single one of the forty places the teammate was worried about, because the constructor's required parameter list never grew.
Only the small number of enterprise-customer code paths that actually need fraud detection have to call the new setter at all, and the rest of the codebase never even has to know it exists.
3. A Practical Decision Test
1. Can the object work correctly without this dependency?
If the answer is no, the dependency is required and belongs in the constructor.
For example, an OrderService without an OrderRepository or PricingEngine cannot do its job at all. The object should not even be created without them.
2. Would forcing it into the constructor hurt callers that don't need it?
If most callers would have to pass null, a dummy object, or some placeholder just to satisfy the constructor, the dependency is probably optional.
For example, only a few enterprise customers may use FraudDetectionService. Forcing every caller to provide it creates unnecessary complexity.
3. Does the dependency need to change after the object is created?
Required dependencies rarely change during the object's lifetime. They are usually fixed once the object is constructed.
If a dependency might be added later, replaced, or reconfigured while the object is already running, it is a good candidate for setter injection.
4. Common Mistakes
Mistake 1: Putting an optional dependency in the constructor
This forces every caller to provide something they may never use. Over time, constructors become bloated and difficult to maintain.
Mistake 2: Using setter injection for a required dependency
The object can be created in a broken state and may fail later because someone forgot to call the setter. Constructor injection prevents this problem entirely.
Mistake 3: Forgetting to handle a missing optional dependency
If a dependency is optional, the code that uses it must first check whether it was actually provided. Otherwise, runtime errors can occur.
Mistake 4: Mixing styles inconsistently
If some required dependencies use constructors and other required dependencies use setters, it becomes difficult to understand which dependencies are guaranteed to exist and which are optional.
5. Quick Reference
Constructor Injection: Use it when the dependency is required and the object cannot work without it.
Setter Injection: Use it when the dependency is optional and can be added or changed later.
Car Analogy: An engine is required and installed at the factory. A roof rack is optional and can be added later.
Decision Rule: Ask three questions:
["Can the object work without this dependency?","Would forcing it into the constructor hurt callers that don't need it?","Does the dependency need to change later?"]
items: Can the object work without this dependency?
Would forcing it into the constructor hurt callers that don't need it?
Does the dependency need to change later?

blocks.content: Choosing the wrong approach causes problems either way: optional dependencies make constructors painful, while required dependencies behind setters allow broken objects to exist.
